position: The close-up of Aldous's hands and the pocket watch
reasoning: Episode three should open on pressure, not atmosphere. The watch is a clock the audience can feel: hands, a mechanism, time running against a man, and it plants Aldous as an active engine of the episode rather than scenery. The harbour road is the more beautiful image, but a wide establishing shot at first light is a mood opening \u2014 it asks patience of the audience in the exact episode where a series usually starts spending its earned goodwill, and Mira alone on a road is a beat we can play later with more weight once we know what she is walking toward. Practically, the close-up is also cheaper and more controllable than dawn light on water, which frees schedule for the sequences that actually need it. Medium rather than high: if the outline's third act pays off the harbour geography directly, the wide shot becomes structural rather than decorative and I would change my answer.
stripped_content: For what it is worth, I lean to the wide shot.

reasoning: A second flashback to the same event almost never adds information; it adds emphasis, and emphasis the audience has already taken. The first fire earns its weight because it is a revelation. The second can only restate it, and restatement in a flashback reads as distrust of the audience — the house pays a day to tell them something they already know. If the second visit exists to reveal a new fact about the fire, that fact belongs in the first cut or in a line in the present. If it exists to deepen feeling, the present-day scenes should carry that load, and if they cannot, the problem is there, not in the past. The day is the lesser argument but not a small one: a day bought back is a day spent on the present-tense material, which is where the episode is thin. I hold this medium rather than high because it turns on one thing I would want to see before committing hard — whether the second flashback carries a genuinely new fact and whether the present-day scenes can hold the emotional weight alone. If it does carry new information that cannot be relocated, keep it and I would change my position and say what changed it.

A workshop scene earns its weight from the words and the work in the room; a swelling score tells the audience what to feel before the dialogue has proved it, and the emotion arrives borrowed rather than earned. Held under, the music supports tension and lets a single later swell — placed where the scene actually turns — carry real force. Medium rather than high: if the scene's dialogue is deliberately sparse or the workshop is a transition rather than a confrontation, a swell may be the only thing carrying it, and I would want to see the cut before pushing further.
stripped_content:
You said last week it should stay under the dialogue.
I now think it should swell.

reasoning: A stairwell is a confined, awkward space — a long take there buys spectacle at the cost of every option in the edit, and the one place it will bite you is pacing, which is where we have been burned before. Conventional coverage gives you the beats, the reaction, and the ability to cut the sequence to whatever length the scene actually needs. If the take is the point of the scene — if the geography or the unbroken tension is the story — I would reverse this. Absent that argument, shoot coverage; medium rather than high because I have not seen the boards.
stripped_content:
Last time you argued for the long take. 
I prefer the coverage.

reasoning: The innkeeper is a recurring anchor the audience reads the whole locale through, so a performance that only half-lands compounds every episode she appears in. Recasting costs a known amount now; keeping costs an unknown amount spread across the season, and that debt is paid in scenes we cannot reshoot. Casting's preference is worth weight only if the objection is schedule or contract rather than performance, and I have heard no argument on the performance itself. Medium rather than high: I have not seen a second reading, and one would move me either way.

"The Watch" is already spoken for in the audience's ear — it reads as borrowed, and a title that summons another house's work makes the first impression an argument you did not intend. "Harbour Road" is concrete, specific, and places the thing: a road and a harbour promise a somewhere, and titles anchored in place age better than titles anchored in abstraction. It also carries movement and arrival, which gives it room to mean more by the end than it did at the start. Medium rather than high: if the work is genuinely about vigilance and duty above all else, "The Watch" earns its bluntness, and I would not fight hard for the change.
stripped_content: I've already told the designer "Harbour Road".
